I am rising to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I should like to pay tribute to the city from which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) comes. It has produced perhaps the best team the world has known. They have gone through their league in splendid form. It may be that some day when I become a cabinet minister I will allow a private member to pay tribute to my city. The Port Arthur Bruins have gone through the finals of this league in four straight games. The outstanding feature of this team is that they are home brews and Simon-pures. That is something which cannot be said of any other team in Canada. Of course an outsider could not have any chance of getting a place.
On Saturday night I saw this team play, and I thought they were called by the wrong name. They should be called antelope or deer instead of bruins.

I rise to a point of order. I have no objection to the motion being moved, and no objection to the house agreeing to the motion if it wishes to do so; but it does seem to me that it requires forty-eight hours' notice. Standing order 45 provides:
Forty-eight hours' notice shall be given of a motion for leave to present a bill, resolution or address, for the appointment of any committee, or for placing a question on the order paper, but this rule shall not apply to bills after their introduction, or to private bills, or to the times of meeting or adjournment of the house. Such notice shall be laid on the table before six o'clock, p.m., and be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of that day.
The only phrase in that order which might be claimed by the hon. member as an exemption is the reference to notice not being required for private bills. The reason notice is not required for the introduction of private bills is obvious; private bills are presented to parliament by petition, but that is all that exemption covers. I go further and quote citation 357 of Beauchesne, second edition:
As a general rule every motion proposed in the house requires notice unless it is of a formal or uneontentious character, or raises a question of privilege.
Further I quote citation 321 from Beauchesne, third edition:
In the absence of standing orders to the contrary, the following motions may be made without notice:
I will not take the time of the house to read the kinds of motions that may be made without notice, listed under citation 321, but they do not include a motion such as this for placing something back on the order paper. As I have said already, I have no objection to the motion being made; in fact I think the house might grant the hon. member this concession. But my point of order is that if the hon. member is seeking by this means to reinstate something on which the house has already ruled, even if in committee of the whole, that makes it a contentious matter. If on the other hand he is prepared to assure the house that he is not seeking to reinstate the name of the company which was rejected by the committee, then it would be uncontentious and I should be willing to waive the requirement of notice.

I thought I would make a brief explanation of the bill, and then, after it is given second reading, ask that it go to the banking and commerce committee, where it can be further studied.
This bill amends the Loan Companies Act, 1927, mainly in respect to the powers of investment and the power to borrow money. However, there are a number of minor amendments. I might say the powers which will go similarly to all companies include the power to elect an executive committee of the board of directors; to establish branch offices; to reduce the par value of the company's stock from $100 to $10 or multiples of $10; to invest in common stork of no par value, of course with limitations; to increase their powers to accept

In view of the intention of the government to send this bill to the banking and commerce committee I shall add only a word or two. It seems to me that in general this bill is designed to give a little more flexibility, and for that reason I approve of it, in general terms. In these days of increasing restrictions it is pleasant to find something which, as I say, appears to give a little more flexibility.
My own feeling is that we can far better rely upon the judgment and capacity of responsible people given a certain amount of freedom than if we try to check them at every turn. In those happy, far-off days when even in Great Britain-perhaps I should say especially in Great Britain-there was a large measure of freedom, I remember a story of what happened to a business associate of mine. Many years ago he went to establish in England a branch of the company he served here in Canada. There he took legal advice, asking what rules he had to comply with and what were the restrictions. He was told there were practically none; then this significant addition was made. His legal adviser said, "You have very few restrictions of any kind. But we have laws in this country, and if you disobey any of those laws you will be put in jail." That is a salutary sanction to have behind those who are conducting the affairs of the country, and it seems to me that is a good rule. I feel sorry they have had to depart from it in Britain to the extent that seems necessary at the present time.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, since it seems to me this measure in general moves in the direction of a certain flexibility and perhaps a little more freedom, I shall reserve any further comments until we get to the banking and commerce committee, where questions may be asked.

Loan Companies Act
There are several features of this amending bill which I do not like and which require some explanation. However, I do not desire to oppose second reading, and shall not do so. Another amendment I do not like is in regard to inspection of the books of the company. Under this change an execution creditor of a shareholder is to be entitled to look into the books. That is what I am objecting to-an examination of the share register of the company so far as an execution creditor of a shareholder is concerned. subtopic: RATES OF PENSION FOR DISABILITY AND DEATH- SALARIES OF PENSION COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as hon. members are aware, Bill No. 126 has been before the committee on veterans affairs since early in the year. From time to time since early in March the committee has submitted to the house certain recommendations, as its deliberations have taken place. I thought I might make some reference to those recommendations.
Pension Act

On March 3 a formal report was made to the house dealing only with matters respecting a quorum and the suspension of standing order 65.
On March 24 the chairman of the committee reported to the house as follows:
Your committee recommends that the government consider the advisability of introducing, at the appropriate time, an amendment to Bill 126, an act to amend the Pension Act, in respect to helplessness allowance to provide that the maximum amount payable to a disabled veteran in any of the classes described ini the scale of helplessness allowance, as at present authorized, be increased from $756 to $1,400 per annum, and that the minimum amount so payable be increased from $250' to $480 per annum.
On April 20 a further report, involving a recommendation for an administrative change, was made. That report is as folows:
Your committee recommends that, upon increases in war disability pension rates going into effect, the Canadian pension commission review each award in payment under section 21 of the Pension Act without the necessity of application by the pensioner.
That was purely an administrative proposal for the pension commission, without the necessity for an amendment to the act.
On April 27 the chairman of the committee reported to the house as follows:
Your committee recommends that the government consider the advisability of introducing, at the appropriate time, an amendment to Bill 126, an act to amend the Pension Act, to provide an increase of twenty-five per centum in the amounts set forth in schedules A and B to the Pension Act.
Your committee further recommends that the government also introduce an amendment to the said Bill 126 to remove the discrimination as to rank contained in subsection two of section twenty-six of the Pension Act.
Finally yesterday, May 10, the chairman reported as follows:
Your committee has considered Bill 126, an act to amend the Pension Act, and has agreed to report it without amendment.
Your committee is of the opinion that the rates provided in certain clauses of the bill are inadequate and that the limitations imposed in other clauses are unduly restrictive. As any revision of these rates to meet the view's of the committee would result in an increased charge upon the public, your committee feels that it has no option, under the rules of the house and the terms of its order of reference, but to report the clauses without amendment. The committee would, however, urge that consideration be given to the recommendations contained in its second and fourth reports presented on March 24 and April 27, respecting rates of helplessness allowance and of war disability pensions, and would also recommend that the government consider the advisability of introducing further amendments to the said Bill 126 to provide:

1.	That, in respect of world war I pension awards, no reduction in the assessment of disability shall be made, provided such assessment has been in effect for three years or more.
2.	That section 11(1) (e) of the Pension Act he amended by striking out all the w'ords after the word "forces" in line twelve thereof and substituting therefor the -words "was obvious on enlistment."
3.	That schedule A to the Pension Act be amended to provide that payment of pensions be made at the nearest multiple of "5r" except where the disability is less than 5 per cent, for which compensation 'by way of a final payment is provided.
4.	That sections 32 and 32A of the Pension Act be amended by striking out the proviso respecting marriage before Mayr 1, 1944, where-ever it appears in these sections; and that section 66 be repealed.
5.	That section 62 of the Pension Act be amended by deleting the words "be entitled to draw and shall" in the fifth line thereof.
It gives me great pleasure to announce that, following a full and most intensive consideration of the representations made before the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs, and after studying the evidence presented there, the government has agreed to accept the recommendations, including an over-all increase of 25 per cent in the basic rates under the Pension Act. Hon. members will be gratified, I am sure, by this decision; for the country has shown clearly its opinion that those who have suffered as a result of death or disability from war service should be adequately compensated.
Perhaps the committee would be interested in a more complete summary of the major items in connection with the recommendations I have read.
Under the proposed new set-up a man and his wife will receive, in the case of 100 per cent disability, a total of $125 monthly as compared with the old rate of $100 monthly. Of this new amount, approximately $94 is payable on behalf of the man and $31 on behalf of his wife. They will receive for their first child $19 monthly, with $15 for the second. The payment for the third and each subsequent child will be at the rate of $12 monthly. This means that in the case of a Canadian family of a man, wife and three children, the total 100 per cent pension will be $171 monthly clear of income tax. This compares with the previous total of $137.
The basic rates for widows of those who have died are increased correspondingly. Instead of the previous payment of $60 monthly, a widow will now receive $75 and the additional allowances mentioned already for any dependent children. The rates for orphan children, following the same principle, will be $38

Pension Act
monthly for the first orphan child, $30 monthly for the second and $24 per month for the third and each subsequent child.
The government has also agreed with the unanimous recommendation of the special committee to a substantial increase in the additional pension paid to those pensioners who unfortunately are totally disabled, helpless and in need of attendance. The previous maximum of $750 a year has been increased to $1,400 a year. This means that a totally disabled pensioner in need of constant attendance will receive, if a married man with no children, $1,500 per year as pension and $1,400 per year as a helplessness allowance, cr a total from both sources of $2,900 annually, none of which is subject to income tax.
Hon. members may be interested in what this will mean in the total annual liability to our country. Under the present rates Canada's annual pension bill for disability pensioners and for dependents is approximately $73 million. This new schedule will increase the bill by $18,000,000 annually and will make a total yearly pension liability of approximately $91 million. The increased benefits resulting from these changes in the basic rates and in the helplessness allowance will be retroactive to October 1, 1947, and immediate action will be taken by the Canadian pension commission and the chief treasury officer to get the adjustment cheques and increased rates of award into payment.
I have already referred to the purely administrative recommendations, but I shall repeat them. The third report recommended that the pension commission review each award under section 21 without the necessity of application by the pensioner. That has been accepted by the government and has gone into effect as an administrative change.
In the fifth report the committee recommended :
That, ini respect of world war I pension awards, no reduction in the assessment of disability shall be made, provided such assessment has been in effect for three years or more.
That administrative policy likewise will go into effect. The other recommendations in the fifth report which was tabled yesterday require amendments to the bill. In the main these will be dealt with by amendments as we deal with the bill in detail. As these amendments involve a number of changes, normally I would have suggested that the bill be reprinted; but knowing it- was the wish of the parliamentary committee, as it is my wish, I asked that this be brought up before the committee of the whole today.
I shall undertake to attempt to answer any questions and deal with each section carefully as amendments are put forward. I assure hon. members that if the bill passes the committee of the whole and receives third reading I shall undertake to see that a reprinted bill is made available.
May I say further that the recommendations contained in the fifth report tabled yesterday have been accepted to an appreciable extent, and additional amendments to the Pension Act will be moved as supplementary clauses to Bill No. 126.
The first amendment deals with the phrase "wilfully and deliberately concealed" in section 11(1) (c), and the inclusion of a definition of the phrase "recorded" on medical examination prior to enlistment. That is a slight variation only from the recommendation of the parliamentary committee.
Second, there will be an amendment to schedule A of the Pension Act to provide that payment of pensions be made at the nearest multiple of "5" except where the disability is less than 5 per cent, for which compensation by way of a final payment is provided.
Third, there wrill be an advancement of the deadline respecting marriages and births from May, 1, 1944, to May 1, 1948, for veterans of world war I. This implements in part the recommendation of the committee. The government does not consider that it is expedient at this time to remove the deadline entirely. This action will take care of cases which gave a great deal of concern to the parliamentary committee.
Fourth, an amendment to section 62 of the Pension Act to provide for the deletion of the words "be entitled to draw and shall" in the fifth line of the section.

At the outset I wish to say that I think the committee will. be greatly pleased that so many of the recommendations have been implemented by the government through the minister. There was almost universal assent to most of these recommendations. We pressed hard in the committee for them and we are pleased indeed that the government has seen fit to implement most of our recommendations. I am not going to touch on the recommendations now, except the one which has to do with schedules A and B, which, after all, is the most important part of the bill to the soldier.
First let me point out that there has been no increase in the pension since 1925, some twenty-three years ago, and I am sure that every member of the house will agree that an increase in pensions is long overdue. During the depression and during the second world war the returned soldier from the first war was quite willing to accept what was coming to him and made very little complaint. In the second world war nearly everyone at home was employed at high wages; but the returned soldier who was unable to work, though many of them did, was content to carry along on his full pension of $75 a month and made no complaint. During the depression, from 1929 to 1937 or 1938, there was also very little complaint from the veterans in this country, although certain benefits which they had been receiving were reduced.
Undoubtedly war workers received very high wages, and, since the war, let it be said to the credit of the veterans organizations throughout Canada that their first concern has been for the rehabilitation of the young soldier returning home rather than pressing for ben-fits for themselves. But now that the young soldier has been more or less re-established on his farm, or in business, or attending school, the older veteran felt that, in duty to himself and to those who stood in need of increased benefits, something should be done to meet their requirements.

Just before the Christmas vacation the Prime Minister announced to the house that there would be an increase of ten per cent in the basic pension. We remember how that announcement was received by members of the house and by the people of this country from one end to the other. It was spoken of as a most ridiculous offer, which it was, and of course the legion and other veterans organizations could not and would not consider it for a moment. Then the bill now before us, Bill No. 126, was introduced, proposing an increase in the basic rate of pension by 16] per cent. This increase was also considered to be m-rf unsatisfactory by members of the house and throughout the country. It was an increase which it was felt should not be considered at all by members of the house and by the different veterans organizations.
When the bill came before the committee a number of recommendations and motions were made. One motion which I had the honour of moving in the committee was to increase the basic pension by 33] per cent. It was put to a vote in the committee and fifteen members voted in favour of the 33] per cent increase and sixteen against, so it was lost by just one vote. After seeing how that 33] per cent vote went, the committee voted unanimously for an increase of 25 per cent. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that while a 25 per cent increase was recommended by one veterans organization, the Canadian Legion, every other veterans organization across Canada had recommended an increase of 33] per cent, and in addition mayors of municipalities and responsible civic organizations from one end of this country to the other sent in to the committee and to the members of the House of Commons many recommendations and petitions for an increase in the pension of 33] per cent.
It might be asked, on what grounds was the 33] per cent increase in the pension based? In that connection I should like to read what the Prime Minister said when he introduced this matter in the house on December 19. At page 489 of Hansard he said:
It was recognized that account should he taken of increases in the general level of wages and salaries since the establishment of the existing rates.
Again, the Minister of Veterans Affairs said at page 63 of the proceedings of the veterans affairs committee:
That was one factor, of course, but there were other factors in relationship to the whole picture of Canada as was mentioned this morning. The living standards of others of the Canadian population were considered by the government, and one might say, as far as it was

Pension Act
possible, all the departments within the government were consulted to see what would be equitable at this time in the light of what can be done.
There were three factors which it was felt should be considered in any increase in the basic rate of pension: first, the cost of living; second, the wage increase across Canada; and third, the increase in the standard of living between 1925 and 1948. Taking first the increase in the cost of living, I think it will be agreed that that is one of the most important factors entering into any proposed increase in the pension rate. While there has been no increase in the basic pension from 1925 until the present time, instead of taking 1925 as the basic year I feel that we would be more justified in taking the year just before the war, say 1939. I say that because the young soldier who fought in the second world war and was mostly concerned with becoming re-established, building a home, buying furniture and meeting household expenses, based his idea of the value of a pension on its worth in 1939, and not 1925, a year which he knew absolutely nothing about.
If we take 1939 as the basis, the cost of living has increased since then to 150-4. Thus it has not increased 33J per cent; it has increased over 50 per cent. Clothing, which is one of the largest elements that enter into the cost of living, has increased to 172-9, or almost 80 per cent. Home furnishings, which is something that the veteran settling down finds an important item, has increased to 161-9. Food has increased to over 169. I just noticed a Canadian Press dispatch in the Montreal Gazette this morning, which spoke about a further rise in the cost of living. The article said:
Cost of living indexes for eight Canadian c-ities April 1 showed increases varying from 1-3 points for Vancouver to 0-4 for Saint John, X.B., the bureau of statistics reported today.
Food and clothing increases were mainly responsible for the advances.
That is the point I wish to emphasize, Mr. Chairman; food and clothing increases are mainly responsible for the advance in the cost of living. Then again the Canadian Press on May 4 said:
Cost of living index goes up to record peak. Advance appears to have steadied; freight rate impact not shown.
The article goes on to say:
The cost of living index, calculated on the basis 1935-39 equals 100, now is at its highest point in history. Before this year the peak was 150-6, established in the inflationary period after the first world war. This record was shattered in February when a 0-8 point boost in that month lifted it to 150-8.
The article also says:
Clothing and food indexes showed the greatest changes between March and April, although small advances were registered also by fuel and light, home furnishings and services and miscellaneous items.
I would point out that there are a lot of small things that we do not think of when we consider the cost of living. For instance, if we go out to buy a paper in the morning, instead of getting it for two or three cents as we did twenty or twenty-five years ago, today we have to pay five cents. This may seem a small matter, but it is indicative of how the cost has gone up in practically everything that we have to buy. I remember when we used to buy the Saturday Evening Post for five cents. That was twenty-five years ago. Today we have to pay fifteen cents. I might mention haircuts and shoeshines, and all these little things. I doubt whether they are included in the cost of living, but they have gone up, not 33^ per cent but 50 per cent, 100 per cent, and in many cases more than 100 per cent. Therefore, so far as the cost of living is concerned, the veteran is more than entitled to a 33i per cent increase in his pension.
The next item which was mentioned as entering into the increase in pension was the rise in wages all across Canada. I would point out that while there was a large increase in wages for workmen in skilled and unskilled labour, ranging anywhere from 50 per cent to 75 or 100 per cent, the pensioner's pension still remains at the same rate as it was in 1925. Speaking about the increase in wages, I should like to refer to a report which was given to our committee by the bureau of statistics. Under the heading, "Wage rates- unskilled factory labour-male", we find that taking 1925 as the standard year at 100, in 1947 the wage rate had increased to 197-4. That is, wages of unskilled factory labour, male, on the basis of 100 in 1925, had almost doubled in 1947. It had increased from 109 to 197-4. If we take the year 1939 and compare it with 1925, we find that it had increased to 108-2. Therefore, from 1939 to 1947 there has been an increase of almost 90 per cent.
I now come to the average earnings of wage and salaried workers. The year 1925 is again-given as the standard at 100. In 1947 wages of the salaried workers had increased to 179, or almost 80 per cent. Therefore, in the matter of the increase in wages, which was the other main factor that should enter into* an increase in pension, we find that unskilled labour had almost doubled its rate from 1925,
Pension Act

and the salaried wage earner's wages had gone up 80 per cent.
The other factor which I feel should enter into an increase in the veteran pensioner's pension is the standard of living. I mentioned that a few moments ago. No action was taken on the standard of living at all. We all know there has been a great increase in the standard of living since 1925. Things that were considered luxuries in those days, such as electrical equipment and so on, are necessities today, and have added greatly to the cost of living so far as the veterans are concerned. I know there are some who will say that the Canadian Legion recommended the 25 per cent increase. That is a fact. The Canadian Legion did recommend 25 per cent, but I would point out to the committee that their recommendation was made some time ago, and that the cost of living has gone up steadily since. They made their recommendation before the beginning of the year and, as we know, the increase has gone up steadily since that time. I should also like to quote from the brief of the Canadian Legion. They make this statement:
Disability pensions are compensation for injuries or disabilities suffered as a result of war service. It was never intended that they should be at bare subsistence level. Awards are based upon medical advice as to the individual's capacity to take employment in the common labour market. It is reasonable, therefore, to expect that a 100 per cent pensioner should receive compensation at least equivalent to the wage paid' for common labour. On an average throughout Canada this would not be less than $100 per month, reckoning on the basis of an hourly rate of 55 cents and an eight-hour day.
I would point out to the committee that the legion was wrong in the assumption that the wage paid for common labour is $100 a month, and that the basic hourly rate is fifty-five cents. As a matter of fact, we were told by officials from the bureau of statistics that the weekly rate of wage was $38 odd which would bring the total up to over $150 a month. We were also told that that included not only men who were heads of families but women and boys. Therefore the legion was basing its recommendation on a wrong assumption. It based its recommendation on the assumption of fifty-five cents an hour for an eight-hour day and $100 a month; but mark you, in its brief the legion says that the totally disabled pensioner should not receive less than $100 a month. I cannot reconcile the recommendation of the legion for a 25 per cent increase when the legion itself says that the soldier should not receive less than $100 a month. I sometimes wonder if the legion was not perhaps a little bit confused over the 25 per cent and the $25 increase. As far back

as July 7, 1947, the general secretary of the Canadian Legion sent a circular letter to all members of the House of Commons. I am not going to read the letter, but attached to it was a recommendation which the legion made at that time. I should like to read an excerpt from it, as follows:
The present rate for a single man-
That is speaking of disability pension.
-is $75 and for a married man $100 per month with additional allowances for children. The more children there are in a pensioner's family, the greater becomes the problem of maintaining a household, notwithstanding family allowances.
The legion's proposal, therefore, would provide the single man with $109 per month and the married man with $125, plus children's pension and family allowances. We believe that such an increase is necessary if unemployable disabled veterans are to be relieved from the exceedingly straitened circumstances under which some are presently existing.
As you see, Mr. Chairman, there again we have the legion recommending the $100, or the increase of 33J per cent. I am satisfied that if that recommendation were justified on July 7, 1947, it is much more justified at the present time. This makes the veterans organizations across the country practically unanimous in their request that a 3.3' per cent increase be given in pensions. I am not going to emphasize this matter any further.
We are pleased indeed that the government has seen fit to increase the pension by 25 per cent. I will say that I believe it has been done under pressure as far as the government is concerned. A few months ago the government offered 10 per cent; then, when they found that it was received across this country with such utter contempt, they increased it to 16J per cent and prepared a bill on that basis. Now they come before us with 25 per cent. That is still inadequate, Mr. Chairman. It is not as much as this country can afford. As the minister told us just a few moments ago, the cost will be something in the neighbourhood of $18,000,000 to give the veterans of this country a 33^ per cent increase; or to give them $100 -which is small pay; no labourer in this country today is trying to live on $100 a month- will cost this government only another $6,000,000.
When we consider that the Minister of Finance, when he brings down his budget, will show a surplus of some $800,000,000, I think, as did the members of the committee, with the exception of one, there should be an increase of 100 per cent for the veterans of this country. Now is the time to give justice to these men. We have not amended these schedules for some twenty-three years. If we do not amend them

Pension Act
again for another twenty-three years, this will be left as it is. I believe that an adequate increase should be given to these men now. In justice I feel that this 25 per cent should be still further amended and that we should give these veterans what they are entitled to.

If I may be permitted to have the floor, Mr. Chairman- with due deference to the hon. member who has just risen-perhaps the house would be kind enough to grant one of the veterans of this chamber the privilege of saying a few words in close proximity to the remarks that have been made by my hon. and gallant friend, the member for Royal. He knows as much about this great problem as many of us, and certainly a great deal more than those of us who might be laymen and who, perhaps through no fault of their own, did not have the high privilege of being part and parcel of the armed services in world war I and world war II.
I thought perhaps you, Mr. Chairman, and the House of Commons might be indulgent to one who has been privileged-as a layman, not as a soldier-to serve as an ordinary individual in Canada who looks on the great work the members of the armed forces did, how they saved democracy for us and how, during the last quarter of a century, they have done their best, as they are doing now, to carry on shoulder to shoulder with the rest of us who have an ambition to be good citizens in this greatest country and nation of the *world, our Canada.
To serve in that manner has been my privilege. I say to the minister who is guiding this legislation through the house, that is something which we think about from day to day, week to week, month to month and year to year when we come in contact with those highly privileged men who saved us. While they wero doing their job, we tried in our humble way to do something on behalf of Canada, but rarely had an opportunity to express our views with regard to their anxieties and with regard to what they had done on our behalf.
I trespass on the time of this committee today to give, in a few sentences, the ideas
of those who are off to one side and who got in on the tail-end of the procession of the boys who deserve the head of the line. The minister, whose deputy I see in front of him, knows that some of us were privileged to give service to those who served us so well and saved our way of life. For that we ask no thanks. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the five or more I see in this chamber who know, that we were privileged to give service; and the minister or his deputy can correct me if I am wrong.
In my own little community of Toronto we were highly privileged to give service to perhaps 4,000 or 5,000 who came back to us maimed and who needed service of a kind that a hospital organization, of which it was my privilege to be chairman, was able to give. The assistance of the Department of Veterans Affairs in our voluntary work is now gratefully acknowledged. They cooperated with this group of sixteen or eighteen men who gave these services to a maximum of servicing two hundred or so veterans daily who returned -during world war II; and how we gloried in being able to do something for them!
That is past, but some things that are past should not be forgotten, and that is why I mention it. That is not the problem just now. Many things run through my mind in trying to follow the able and gallant speech, if that is a proper word, of the hon. member for Royal, who is a gallant man in common with many of my associates whom I see in this chamber. These gallant men must have within their very hearts and souls the needs of those who have been privileged to return. We ordinary men may not be able to appreciate the situation as they do, though I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and through you the minister to remember that some of our blood also served.
Apart, from that, we as humble citizens have tried our utmost to see their point of view. For a quarter of a century I have had these men and their wives coming to my door. Any time I am at home the door is open to them after seven o'clock in the evening. I have learned to love, admire and respect these men and women, and I am anxious to be of some service to them. But I also think of others with whom it has been my privilege to come in contact, a few hundred employees in a plant where we have never had a strike or trouble of any kind. For years I have listened to their woes, to their family troubles, and so forth. In Calgary we have twenty or thirty, in Toronto another three hundred and fifty, and all those people
Pension Act

know there is one individual to whom they can come with their difficulties. None of this group have troubles with respect to pensions. Their difficulty is that they are not pensioned enough, that they are not earning enough, that they should have more money, better housing, and so on, running the whole gamut of those things which enter into our daily life.
I am privileged perhaps even more than the hon. member for Royal and many other members of this house to hear the story of the ordinary civilian and also to hear the story of the veteran and his wife and family. For a long period it has been my pleasure to provide payrolls for these people; and having some idea of costs, I say quite frankly and sincerely that during the last quarter of a century the amounts we have paid men incapacitated one hundred per cent, and on down the line, along with the pensions that went to their widows and families, which in the early days might have been on a par with what obtained in ordinary civilian life, have gradually lost that relationship.
I do not charge the minister with responsibility for this. I say it has been the responsibility of this chamber, Canada's House of Commons, that these pensions have not kept pace with rising costs of all kinds. Just last Sunday I received telephone calls from three returned soldiers in my own community, one a veteran of the first war and two veterans of the second war. They said their rents had been almost doubled. They were carrying on ordinary little grocery stores in that vicinity, and suddenly they found their rents greatly increased. I could give the figures; perhaps from $55 to $100, which is not quite double, or from $85 to $150, again not quite double, but that is not necessary to quote. The fact is that the cost of remaining in their places of business and keeping their families together has been almost doubled.
Not only that, but many times I am asked questions like this. "Where am I to live? I have two rooms, and they are costing me $40 a month. I do not know where to go for more room." Someone may say, as I sometimes do, that in the rural parts of Ontario we have thousands of vacant farm homes; so why should these people not go and rehabilitate those farms? That might be all right for my worn-out employee who has an aptitude for farming, or for thousands of others who should go back to the land; but I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that the men for whom the minister is responsible, because of their training, their war service, and in many cases their disabilities, are not able to go on the land in Canada. They are city bred and soldier trained; they

are accustomed to army food and army life, and you cannot change them overnight. These are not people you can transplant to vacant farm houses anywhere. They should have the first call on any available work in our cities and towns, for a dozen reasons.
The other group who have not served overseas, many of whom were brought to this country from Europe because of their training on farms, could be dealt with in a different way. If there were some squeeze process which could force foreigners to go to the vacant farms of Ontario and the other provinces, I would be ready to vote for that squeeze to be applied; but I would not be prepared to say this should be done in the case of our own citizens who served in the second great war, who perhaps came right out of high school, with no idea at all of agriculture and whose fathers were perhaps tradesmen. I am not suggesting they should be pushed out of the larger centres. But I would urge, as forcefully as I am able, that we be placed in a position where we can demand that those who have not served our national needs, those who have not served us in helping save democracy, be asked to get out of the way. Others should be made to vacate some of the homes they are occupying, and some of the positions they hold, to make room for those of our boys who have graduated from the schools and who, in the best years of their lives, served overseas.
Bring those young men into wholesome communities where, in their turn, they can make a living. We hear talk about increases in costs. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to think about those increases in costs. I ask the same of any member who has had the privilege of making up a payroll each Friday night. I look at the costs of 1935, and compare them with those of today; I look at those of 1939, and again compare them with present costs.
A few moments ago I heard the hon. member for Royal make a reference to a payment of fifty-five cents an hour. As an ordinary manufacturer, I thought of the good old days when we paid fifty-five cents an hour; and we did not show many deficits.
Let us consider the ordinary labourer today. Perhaps he is not able to read or write. All he knows is how to punch a time-clock at eight o'clock each morning, change his clothes, and start to work at about eight-fifteen. He will wait around, work along and slog around until about a quarter to twelve. Let us not forget that about ten o'clock he has a rest period of five or ten minutes. Then, after lunch he comes back at one o'clock to resume his work; and I should not like to say how many minutes after one o'clock he actually begins. I do not

want a strike in any of my plants. But he does start to work shortly after one o'clock.
I was not here on Friday night; I found it necessary to be absent on some important business. Coming down the stairs at the plant about a quarter to five, I was almost mobbed by men coming upstairs, ready to sign off, with their day's work complete. Work eight hours a day?-well, perhaps seven and a half. I hope they did. And if they did not work seven and a half hours, I am not complaining much.
But what a change! From the time the minister's department-and this was before his term of office-suggested fifty-five cents an hour, we can remember what has taken place. Not one of them draws less than eighty cents an hour, and is paid for eight hours each day. 1 am not going to quibble, but I leave it to the imagination of lion, members to decide how many of those eight solid hours they were actually working from the time they began work at a quarter after eight o'clock in the morning until they stopped at a quarter to five; less, of course, an extra ten minutes at tea, and tea at ten o'clock-about all of which I do not complain.
Thank God we have a Canada here which gives our men all these great privileges. But I am sorry, in a quiet sort of way-

With regard to the matter under discussion, while we are disappointed in some respects, we feel that the government has made a vast improvement over what we were led to expect when we first assembled this session and when the committee on veterans affairs was set up. I have had the privi-

lege of sitting on this committee ever since I came to the House of Commons in 1945. Without casting any reflection upon the previous chairman or minister, I want to say that the present chairman has been most agreeable and able in the conduct of his duties and the minister has been most sympathetic and helpful in the carrying on of the work. The same goes for the officials of his department from whom we got a great amount of information.
I am not going to go into all the matters that were dealt with by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), but I want to refer to one or two things about which I am extremely pleased. I note that the minister is going to move an amendment in order to accept the recommendation of the committee to remove the words "wilfully and deliberately concealed" from section 11(1) (c) of the Pension Act. That is a matter of gratification to myself and a great many other people.
While those words may have been put in the section with the best of intentions, we have always felt that their effect was to create a rather unpleasant connotation when veterans were looking over the act. I want to point out here as I did in the committee that the words "wilfully and deliberately concealed" indicate that someone attempted to get into the army with the expectation of later on exploiting his services in order to live the life of Riley in the future. That is not a good situation.
I remember when I first went to enlist in world war I a number of us came in from the outlying country dressed in our working clothes. The recruiting was done in a rather informal manner because it had not been organized as it was later on. We went before the attestation officer and answered the various questions that were asked with regard to our health. What young man, even though he had a slight disability, would admit it, especially before other young men? That is not what we would expect a human being to do. Others forgot them, while others felt that if they disclosed anything it would be considered that they were trying to back out after having got in the recruiting office.
I think, with these words out, the administration of the act will not lose in efficiency, while a great many veterans will be highly pleased.
I am glad the government has agreed to bringing the pension up to the nearest five per cent if the disability is over the half-way mark. I think administration will be easier. We were all very much in favour of that and we are glad the government has accepted the recommendation.

Pension Act
I was a little disappointed in the minister's announcement with regard to the deadline respecting marriages, which is to be moved from May 1, 1944 to May 1, 1948, which has now passed. If there had to be a deadline, which the committee did not want, I would have thought the government could have moved it forward to 1952 or somewhere about there and then watch the progress of events from that point on. However we are not going to quarrel over that too much; in fact we are not going to quarrel over it at all. I think the striking out of the words "be entitled to draw and shall" from section 62 of the act was necessary, and I do not think that deletion will hamper the operation of the act or its administration. In the course of time I am sure it will have a beneficial effect.
We are glad that the government and the minister have accepted the recommendation that no reduction in assessment of disability shall be made, provided that such assessment has been in effect for three years or more. That will be a tremendous improvement over the old act and we are glad to have it.
With regard to the schedules I want to point out that there was a difference of opinion between the two veterans organizations that presented extensive briefs. Like the hon. member for Royal, I am inclined to think that if the legion had given just a little bit more thought to it they likely would have agreed with the recommendations of the national council of veterans associations and would have recommended the 33J per cent. That 33j per cent, if granted, would have amounted to only S100 a month. I do not think any member of this house or anybody outside who has an income of over $100 a month would like to be compelled to live on $100 a month, for a single person. I agree that what we have secured is better than what we were led to expect when we first came here. Nevertheless wc should have been infinitely more pleased had this very minimum of 33J per cent been granted.
Small local governing bodies in this country, village councils, town and city councils, people back in the country who have to collect the taxes from the people they meet every day and are not removed like the taxing authorities here in Ottawa from the people they tax but meet them, as I say, every day, and have to be careful also in the spending of those taxes- responsible bodies of this sort sent in resolutions asking that an increase of 33J per cent be granted; and because I felt that these responsible bodies had given consideration to the cost which would be involved in such an increase and were willing to meet it in their local governments on behalf of their taxpaying citizens, I supported the recommendation to that effect which the hon. member for Royal moved in the committee. But, as he pointed out, it was defeated on a vote by a very small majority. He failed to remind the house that I then immediately moved-and I mention this to keep the record straight- another amendment to the resolution which was then before the committee. Someone asks me to explain what we meant by the 25 per cent increase, plus the cost of living bonus. It would have brought the pension, in round figures, to about 894 a month. If the cost of living index went down a couple of points the pension would have dropped to $100, and if the cost of living index dropped six more points at some time in the future the pension would reach its base, a minimum of $94. Should the cost of living index go higher than it is at the present time, it would mean that the pension would increase accordingly, to perhaps $110 or $115, depending on the rise in the cost of living index. Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 199, to amend the criminal code (juries).
He said: I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to delay the house for more than a few minutes tonight. This particular bill is one of the reasons I think we should have a legal committee in this house for the purpose of considering legal bills. I believe it would save a great deal of the time of the house.
My argument is this. Women can sit in the high court of parliament, in this house and in another place, and they can do many things today that they could not do in years gone by. This bill will make provision for women to be on juries. This matter was brought before the House of Commons last session. One of the cardinal principles of the British constitution is that the courts are subservient to the legislature. It is also one of the cardinal principles of Magna Carta that the people shall take a large share in the administration of criminal justice. One of these matters is the inspection of public institutions. With all due respect to the House of Commons here, I want to say that we are miles behind the old country in the matter of law reform. A committee was set up there shortly before the second great war broke out to consider all phases of this problem, with the result that a bill was prepared, although it was not introduced, embracing many of the features I am proposing here tonight. We are somewhat reluctant to advance one iota from what we had fifty years ago in the way of law reform. Law reform is one of the most important matters which this parliament can deal with.
With regard to the place of women today, I may say that some years ago when I first was head of our city, we found that married women, unless they owned property, could not vote in municipal elections. We went to the legislature and a bill was passed which made provision for two votes in the house, one for the man who was the tenant or the owner and one for his wife. Then in 1917 we went farther. We went to the Ontario government and said that this law had proved good in municipal matters. On account of what women did in the first war, and the suffering they endured, the Ontario legislature adopted the principle of our bill, namely, to give women over twenty-one years of age the right to vote in provincial elections. Toward the close of the first war, on that principle, after a long fight women obtained the federal franchise.
In the election held for this parliament, in June, 1945, fifty-one per cent of the women voted and forty-nine per cent of the men voted. As hon. members know, I believe in law reform, which has been a dead letter
Criminal Code

in Canada as compared with the old country. We shall have some law reform if we pass this bill.
I remember, on one occasion some years ago, going over to the Hull assizes when I first saw the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) in action. There were all men on the jury. He had them all weeping. First, of all, the court crier started to weep. Then some tall fellows at the back of the hall started to weep also. The late minister of justice the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, one of the most beloved men in the province of Quebec, asked me to go over to see this young barrister there, and I did so. The result of this exhibition of sorrow was that court was adjourned until next morning. The jury wept as did everybody else. Everybody had his handkerchief out and all that kind of thing. The result was that a verdict of not guilty was brought in with regard to the prisoner. That is the first time I saw the hon. member for Temiscouata in action.
I do not know how far he is prepared to go with regard to this bill, but I should like to say this. Last session I introduced into the House of Commons a bill to allow women on juries. I believe that if women could secure this part of law reform, it would be a step in the right direction. If a female is being tried, I believe there should be females on the jury. Twenty years ago, when I first brought this matter before the House of Commons in 1927-1028, Mr. Harry Anderson, a popular and able editor, of the Toronto Globe, said he thought women were too temperamental. In my opinion, they are not any more temperamental than some of the men I see in this chamber when votes are being taken.
In the second place, Mr. Speaker, I want to call attention to one fact, and that is the place of women at the present time, and what they are doing in organizations like the Red Cross and the patriotic fund. Even with regard to our elections for this House of Commons, who does most of the work? From what I see of the matter, I think the women do. The men do not work now the way they used to. They leave it to the women in the daytime. Women can sit on the boards of education. There are twenty-five or thirty of them in the British House of Commons. I would point to what they are doing in education and public health, and in the Red Cross and the patriotic fund. Now they can be lawyers. Some are judges, some are magistrates and all that kind of thing. I would also mention what they are doing in organizations like the I.O.D.E., the national council of women, the patriotic fund, 
hospitals and charities, the Red Cross, the schools and churches. They lead in all these good works. By what they have done in two long wars they have earned the place they now have.
Among the most important things, I believe, is the inspection of public institutions; and I believe that women would be better equipped to do this than men. What have we with regard to the inspection of public institutions? We have no inspection at all, except by crown officers. I am not here to say anything against crown officers. They are good and they are not responsible for wffiat goes on. We in the House of Commons are responsible. I can say this. If women inspected some of these institutions such as the Don jail in my constituency, which was built shortly after confederation and has been condemned by grand juries whose reports have just been pigeonholed, changes would be made. I venture to say if women went there and saw what was going on at the present time there would be a vast improvement in no time in the conduct of these public institutions.
Then we see the place women are occupying today with regard to many other matters. I do not wish to detain the house much longer because there may be other members who wish to speak. On the streets of Ottawa these days will be noticed banners urging the public to be kind to animals and to make contributions to the Humane society and all that kind of thing. It seems to me that there should be some kind of society with a slogan, "Be kind to humans."
With regard to the Toronto Humane society, a fine organization according to a clipping I have in my hand, their inspectors went out and examined 134,000 cattle, sheep and swine,
40,000	poultry, 4,300 horses and 19,000 cats; also hundreds of inquiries a week regarding the care of animals are received by the Toronto office. They have issued a pamphlet on the care of animals such as dogs, cats, horses, birds and so on. So far so good.
After every great war there is always dislocation. There is always an outbreak of crime after every great war. The time has now come for these women, who have done such good work during two wars and in the depression, to be given this right. They have proven their case. There is no reason why they should not sit on juries. I venture to say they would be far better than some of the men I have seen on juries, and would bring about real law reform in this country by their inspection of these places.
Then take the question of the inspection of institutions such as the Mercer reformatory

Criminal Code
and other similar buildings which should have been torn down years ago. It is true that under the present minister, Mr. Dunbar, Ontario has announced the opening of certain new institutions to look after the young people of this province who get into difficulties, but as far as the Toronto jail is concerned I see no improvement at all. The city of Toronto was a pioneer in law enforcement. It built a jail farm for young people away out Yonge street north of Thornhill, and another institution for women three miles west of the city, at Concord. The intention was then that the Toronto jail should be closed, but I venture to say it will never be closed under dual control. Today there are dozens of young people. lying on the floors there and not being properly looked after. I do not want it understood that I am criticizing the staff. They are very good, but they operate under antiquated conditions and have to do the best they can.
I venture to say that if women were on the juries and made presentments they would see that something was done about it. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) has made some improvements, no doubt, in federal prisons, but if I had my way I would put a sign over some of these federal institutions: "Abandon hope all ye who enter here". Often those in charge of these institutions have had no training for the work, and as novices, learn only from experience. I am not here to criticize them; far from it, but I believe we should give women the right of inspection when they are serving on juries.
I would not want any sob stuff in this discussion. I believe if these institutions were properly conducted we would see the same results that have been experienced in the old country. I would not urge any reform which is not in the public interest; but look at what is happening in the old land. Under the summary convictions act people are given time in which to pay their fines, instead of being sent to jail. When people are out of work and have not the money with which to pay their fines, they should not have to go to jail. I am shocked at some of the fines imposed in the Toronto police court under our control system, and federal tax matters, sometimes running into thousands of dollars compared with other places. Why, they summon people there for not having a radio licence, and all the rest of it. The administration of these federal laws is a severe charge upon the municipal police systems of the country, and they cannot provide institutions for those people. If we had the law reform they had in England fifteen or twenty years ago, a real summary conviction act; if we gave people time to pay their fines, I believe half 5849-243
the prisons could be closed up here as they were in England.
Our pace has been very slow in this country in regard to prison reform; though some improvements have been made in the last year or two, they are more farcical than real. As far as inspection goes, however, there is none. Members of the House of Commons have the right to inspect these institutions, but how many go there? Hardly any member of this house or any federal minister has inspected one of these institutions, or knows how it is conducted. If women were on the juries I think they would get better results, and for that reason I hope the Minister of Justice will consider accepting these amendments, or widen out the bill for female juries for females. While I have great respect for him and for the attention he has given his duties, I really think we should have some legal committee which, during the recess of parliament, would do what was done in England in 1938, when Sir Robert Horne had a bill all ready to introduce before the war broke out. The bill has now passed both the House of Commons and the House of Lords in England, after elaborate inquiry.
I believe the time has come for real law reform in Canada, and this is one phase of it. I believe women should be allowed to serve on the jury in a case involving another woman; but I really feel that the inspection feature by women is a most important part of it. If women were to inspect some of these institutions, asylums, federal and provincial jails, and so on, I believe we would get some reforms which we cannot seem to get now with juries of men making presentments to the judge, who sends them to the authorities where they are simply pigeonholed.

The answer given by my deskmate is correct. Even the most ardent feminists have not been advocating the superiority of one sex over the other. They have been sponsoring equality. In the administration of justice it would be a guarantee of security to women who may be called upon to appear before the courts to see persons of their own sex deciding their fate.
The exemptions must be different from those concerning men called for jury duty, and the suggestions -made in this bill are perhaps not sufficiently complete, because there should -be another provision with respect to the exemption of women called toi serve on juries. That is, however, an easy matter to adjust. It should not take long to add the dispensation I have in mind.
If I understood correctly what the hon. member for Broadview has said so well, it is that he wants an acceptance of the principle of permitting women to serve on juries. To say that women are temperamental is unjust. They -are no more temperamental than men. Indeed I know many men who are much more temperamental than women. Besides that, as a rule women are better informed -than men, because they read more. Some have achieved success before the bar, on the bench and in many other activities.
I -shall gladly support the hon. member's bill, provided that in due course there is an amendment exempting mothers with young children from the obligation of serving on juries. I am bound to say that in the jurisdiction in which I live there is no demand for it. That is my size-up of the situation. Remember I am in favour of it, but if women do not want the right to serve on juries I do not think we should force it upon them. They are delicate people and they do not appreciate force. I know of no great demand by women's organizations anywhere for the right to serve upon juries.
Those of us who are in the business of trying lawsuits before juries know it is one of the hardest things in the world to get men to serve on them. Unfortunately that is true. I agree with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that it is the cornerstone or pivot, certainly, of a branch of our law. We all believe in jury trials, but those of us who have been engaged in them, and I see quite a number here, will bear me out when I say that you never have a jury trial where you do not get telephone calls or visits from half a dozen people who say, "Please keep me off that jury." I do not care whether you are on the side of the prosecution or the defence, the same applies. That is what is found in actual experience.
Take for instance, coroners' juries. In the place where I live they are all friends of Paddy O'Sullivan who is in charge of coroners' inquests. We see the same boys on those juries all the time. If one of them happens to be sick they even have substitutes out there. It just runs along in that particular way.
We have had great difficulty to get men to serve, and unless there is some considerable opinion among women that they want to serve, I do not see why we should make it obligatory and force it upon them. May I say that I go again with the sponsor of this bill; I go again with the hon. member for Vancouver East, and I say that if we are going into this at all, let us make it complete emancipation. Let there be no difference whatever, where jury service is concerned, between men and women. Let us go the whole way in approving the equality of the sexes about which we have been talking this evening.

maintopic: ONE-THIRD OF JURORS TO BE FEMALE IN TRIAL OF FEMALE PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the bill passes I think I should say something about it. I do not often agree with the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), but on this occasion I agree with him almost completely. What we want in this country are full-fledged citizens who will discharge the duties of citizenship whether they are men or women. I do not think we should

debar women from doing things because they are women. I do not think we should debar them from the professions or refuse to pay them the same wage for doing the same work if they can do the job on the same basis as other people do it. I do not think we should deny them administrative posts because they are women, as we so often do. For instance, I do not think we should let them raise all the money in our churches and then not permit them to sit on church boards or be ministers, as we always do. I do not think we should discriminate against them in one field and then say they must do something in another.
I would hope that as women attained to the full stature of citizenship, as practising democrats and as responsible persons, they would be willing to sit on juries and give jury service in the same way as other citizens give it who happen to be men. I would oppose anything that says you must pick out women because they are women. Also you must not disqualify women because they are women. I would hope that we would permit more women to practise law and become judges. I do not know why we should force women to sit on juries and then tell them that they cannot be judges in any court that amounts to anything. If we give women the full rights of citizenship, then outstanding women should be permitted to be judges or act in the same capacity as other outstanding persons in the legal profession. I could not support anything that discriminates as between men and women in connection with the rights and duties of citizenship.

maintopic: ONE-THIRD OF JURORS TO BE FEMALE IN TRIAL OF FEMALE PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the last two speakers. If the bill had the effect of establishing the equality of men and women I would be ready to support it, but I cannot read that into this bill. As far as New Brunswick is concerned, this bill would be of very little use. I have acted as crown prosecutor in the county of Restigouche for seven years and I do not recall one instance of a woman being brought to trial by jury. There may be isolated cases here and there, but they are few. Of course that is to their credit.
Unfortunately I have not the act here, but in my province we have a provincial jury act the same as other provinces, and in that act the qualifications of jurors are set out. Certain classes of persons are debarred from serving on juries. For instance, barristers are disqualified, and there are other professions which are also disqualified.

Criminal Code

maintopic: ONE-THIRD OF JURORS TO BE FEMALE IN TRIAL OF FEMALE PERSONS
speechtext: And members of parliament.

maintopic: ONE-THIRD OF JURORS TO BE FEMALE IN TRIAL OF FEMALE PERSONS
speechtext:
Yes, members of parliament and medical men. Firemen, if they are not debarred, at least have the privilege of refusing to serve. There are a number of classes who are either debarred from serving on juries or have the privilege of refusing to act. I am wondering whether there is any demand that women should serve on juries. I have heard of no such demand from my province, and if there is no such demand I suggest that we should not interfere with the present state of the law.
As I said a moment ago, in order to make this proposal operative, our present jury act would have to be amended considerably.
The last speaker referred to some sort of handicap under which females suffer in the professions. In my province ladies are admitted to the bar and quite a few of them are actively engaged in the exercise of their profession. We have no female judges as yet, but we may have. I do not think there is anything in any provincial or federal law debarring ladies from being appointed to judgeships.
I have said that I acted as crown prosecutor for a number of years, and there is hardly ever a case, particularly in connection with offences against morals, where the situation in the court room is not at times tense and delicate. It is difficult enough to get ladies who testify to tell the real facts about some unfortunate matters which come before our courts, and I suggest that very few women would enjoy sitting in a juiy box and listening to the dirt that comes out in the evidence in a great many cases. For this reason I am of the opinion that it is no decent place for ladies, even if it is only in connection with the trial of female offenders.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the bill in its present form. I would have no objection perhaps if it were in a more general form, but in its present form I certainly object to it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ONE-THIRD OF JURORS TO BE FEMALE IN TRIAL OF FEMALE PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that I shall have to oppose the bill which the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has introduced, but in doing so I should like to make it clear that I am not at all opposed to the principle of equality of opportunity for jury service as * between men and women, or, as it is expressed in the English act, equality of liability to jury service, because it is ultimately more of a
liability than an opportunity, as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has said.
The debate in the first ten or fifteen minutes seemed to proceed on the assumption that what we are deciding in this bill is the principle of equality of opportunity as between the sexes, but the bill is not as simple as that. The bill is a definite and specific proposal, and that proposal is that there should be in those provinces where the jury consists of twelve, four women on the jury, no more and no less, where the accused is a woman. As some speakers have pointed out, there is something illogical about the rigidity of a provision of that kind. It may be that in some cases the jury should consist entirely of women; it may be that in some cases the jury should consist entirely of men; but certainly I can think of no good argument why there should be four women, no more and no less, on any particular jury. I think the bill is exceedingly faulty in that regard.
If my hon. friend had introduced the principle which was introduced in England about thirty years ago of equality of liability to jury service as between men and women, with the provision that the judge might make exceptions in particular cases, I would say there was a great deal to support that principle in the Dominion of Canada. But then I would have to pass on to certain other features of this bill which we cannot overlook, and the most important of those features is the principle, which has obtained in our system of criminal law and procedure since confederation, of adopting the qualifications of jurors set by the respective provinces.
The British North America Act provides by section 91 that the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to:
27. The criminal law, except the constitution of courts of criminal jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters.
Section 92 provides that the provincial legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to:
14. The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance, and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and of criminal jurisdiction, and including procedure in civil matters in those courts.
As I shall point out a little later, some of the cases raise a doubt as to whether the prescription of qualifications for jurors comes under the heading of procedure in criminal matters or under the heading of constitution, maintenance and organization of the criminal courts. I would not contend, nor would I
Criminal Code

admit that this parliament has not jurisdiction to pass a bill such as my hon. friend proposes. All I can say is that the matter is not free from doubt under the cases as I read them, and I shall refer to that later. I am under the impression, however, that the matter is covered by the heading, "procedure in criminal matters", and is therefore within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament. But whether it is within the jurisdiction of this parliament or not, the question arises, as it so often does, as to the propriety and the desirability of breaking the long practice of relying upon the provisions of the nine provincial jury acts which prescribe the qualifications for jurors. The section which provides for such reliance is section 921 of the criminal code, which reads as follows:
Every person qualified and summoned as a grand or petit juror, according to the laws in force for the time being in any province of Canada shall be duly qualified to serve as such juror in criminal cases in that province.
2. Seven grand jurors, instead of twelve, may find a true bill in any province where the panel of grand juroTS is not more than thirteen.
That section has a long history and, although it may weary the house, I should like briefly to sketch it.
By a statute of the province of Upper Canada passed in 1800, namely 40 George III, chapter 1, the criminal law of England was introduced to the province of Upper Canada as such law stood on September 19, 1792.
By the Upper Canada Jurors Act passed by the parliament of the Province of Canada in 1850, being 13-14 Victoria, chapter 55, a whole code dealing with the qualifications, calling and challenging of jurors was introduced. This act was superseded by "An Act to amend and consolidate the jury laws of Upper Canada", passed by the parliament of the Province of Canada in 1858, being chapter 100 of 22 Victoria. This act repealed all former acts relating to jurors and provided a new jury code covering the whole field of selection, qualification, summoning and challenging of jurors. This act was carried forward into the consolidation of the statutes of Upper Canada of 1859 as chapter 31 thereof.
The act which is a counterpart of the 1859 act in Lower Canada is found in chapter 84 of the consolidation of the statutes of Lower Canada 1860.
Following confederation, the provisions respecting form and challenging of juries formerly in the jurors acts, to which I have referred, passed into "An act respecting procedure in criminal cases and other matters relative to the criminal law", of 1869, being chapter 29 of 32-33 Victoria, while the provisions res-

pecting the qualifications and summoning of jurors passed into the jurors acts of the new provinces. In this connection, the latest preconfederation criminal procedure act was chapter 99 of the statutes of the Province of Canada, 22 Victoria. The Criminal Procedure Act of 1869 provided by section 44 as follows:
44. And for avoiding doubt, it is declared and enacted, that every person qualified and summoned as a grand juror or as a petty juror in criminal cases, according to the laws which may be then in force in any province of Canada shall be and shall be held to be duly qualified to serve as such juror in that province, whether such were laws passed before or be passed after the coming into force of the British North America Act, 1867-subject always to any provision in any act of the parliament of Canada, and in so far as such laws are not inconsistent with any such act.
This provision was carried forward as section 160 of the Criminal Procedure Act in the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1886 as chapter 174 thereof. In the criminal code of 1892 55-56 Victoria, chapter 29, the provision appears as section 662 with the deletion of the explanatory part thereof dealing with laws in force before the province was admitted to confederation. The provision as it now appears in section 921 in the criminal code, first appeared as section 921 in the revision of the code in 1906, being chapter 146 of the revised statutes of that year.
I have traced this sequence very carefully, because it shows clearly that no substantial alteration has been made in this section, which purports to adopt the provincial law in respect to the qualification and summoning of jurors for purposes of criminal law, since first enacted just after confederation.
I have here-possibly I had better not weary the house with it-also an analysis of the other jury sections of the criminal code, sections 922, 923, 924, 925, 926. 927, 928. 929, 930, 931, 932, 933, 935, 936, 937, 938 and 939. I will simply sum up the effects of the research that has been made into the history of these sections by stating the conclusion that is to be drawn from them. My conclusion is, of the nineteen sections of the present code dealing with juries, eleven appeared first in the act passed immediately after confederation in 1869, one deals exclusively with Manitoba, and another with libel. It is safe to say, I think, therefore, that no substantial changes have been made by the federal authority respecting the policy in connection with jurors and juries since confederation. It will also be noted that at no stage since confederation has the federal authority concerned itself with the qualifications of jurors in criminal cases, but rather, this field has been left exclusively to the provinces by virtue of section 921. Sex, being

Privilege-Mr. Gardiner
one of many qualifications, is noticeable by its absence from the criminal code.
It is interesting to examine, for the purposes of comparison, the legislation in England with respect to jurors and juries. The governing act in England is "The Juries Act 1870", being 33 and 34 Victoria, chapter 77. The application of this act, which encompasses special and common juries, is restricted to England and Wales. Section 5 provides that "The word juror shall mean male persons only". The act sets out the qualifications and method of summoning jurors in a manner not dissimilar to many of our provincial acts. "The Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act 1919", being 9 and 10 Geo. V., chapter 71, by section 1 removes disqualification on account of sex or marriage from the exercise of any public function and provides inter alia "A person shall not be exempted by sex or marriage from the liability to serve as a juror." The section further provides:
Any judge ... or other person before whom a case is or may be heard on an application.. . by . . . the parties (including in criminal cases the prosecution and the accused) . . . make an order that the jury shall be composed of men only or of women only ... or may on an application made by a woman to be exempted from service on a jury . . . grant such exemption.
The section further provides that rules of court may be made exempting women for medical reasons.
