subtopic: RATES OP PENSION FOR DISABILITY AND DEATH

speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 126, to amend the Pension Act-Mr. Gregg-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

subtopic: RATES OP PENSION FOR DISABILITY AND DEATH
speechtext:
I
wish to say a few words, Mr. Chairman, on this bill now before the committee. I do not intend to review the many points and arguments so well put forward by the hon. member for Royal this afternoon, except to say that I agree with and concur in all the many points and arguments he raised. Like the hon. member for Royal and the other members who spoke this afternoon, I was happy to hear the minister announce that a 25 per cent increase had been made in the basic rate of pension. While this increase was considerably less than the amount to which the veteran was entitled, and less than the amount he expected, I am sure it will be a source of satisfaction to the members of the present veterans affairs committee in this house to feel that they have been able, through their combined efforts, to obtain this increase for the many veterans.
It appeared to me that it is a strange state of affairs that the government, the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his department could be so much out of touch and out of line with the general feeling in Canada, the feeling of the legion and the veterans themselves, that they believed an increase of |10 a month would be sufficient to meet the increased cost of living or to bring the veterans' pensions more or less up to par with other allowances.
No one will argue, that the veteran has not a legal claim against this country for any disability that he has incurred while in the armed services. When it is remembered that

these veterans have had no increase in well over twenty-three years, that they received no cost of living bonus during the war years, that they had to pay income tax on their pensions, I think they are to be commended because they never thought of or considered making any organized attempt to force the government to raise their pension during the war years. With regard to the veterans' organizations that have appeared before the present veterans affairs committee, in my opinion their demands were moderate in every way, were well advanced and were supported by ample evidence.
It is interesting to note that in at least one province at the present time the total amount allowed for 100 per cent disability under the workmen's compensation act is $100. I mention that because I do not think it is unreasonable to compare the total amount payable in Ontario to a civilian injured in his employment, with the amount paid to a veteran who received his disability in the defence of freedom and of this country.
I am still of the opinion that this country can do much more for the veteran. There has been too much talk in this house and before the veterans affairs committee as to what the cost of this increase is to be. The minister himself, speaking before the veterans affairs committee on April 13, as reported at page 156 of the proceedings, made this significant remark:
Regarding disability pensions, the government cannot see its way clear at this session of parliament to go further than their present proposal, which is now before you.
That proposal was an increase of $10 a month; then there was a second announcement that it would be increased to $12 a month. It might be interesting for the minister, while this bill is before us, to explain to the committee what caused the government and himself to change their minds from April 13 until today when he announced that the increase would be 25 per cent. This is just another illustration of how much out of touch the government and the minister are with the feeling of the veterans and the feeling of the public; because every member in this house has received resolutions, letters, telegrams and briefs from all sorts of bodies, individuals and associations on this matter.
I should also like to ask the minister if he would say, while this bill is before the house, if in his opinion this increase of 25 per cent which he announced this afternoon does justice to the veteran; and if, in his opinion, it is all the veteran is entitled to. I for one still hope that the house will, at some later day, bring forward a further amendment to the Pension

Pension Act
Act, whereby the basic rate will be increased to $100 a month for 100 per cent disability.
The members who served on this commission had the privilege of having appear before them a delegation composed of veterans who had 100 per cent disability. There were blind veterans, veterans with double amputations, paraplegics, and blind veterans with one or two amputations. As I looked at those boys, one thought occurred to me. When you read in the press something about a blind veteran or a paraplegic, it simply does not register on your mind. But when these boys appear before your eyes and speak to you; when they state their case and argue it, when you compare your own whole body with those of these young Canadians appearing before you; when you realize that these boys carry their disabilities twenty-four hours a day and will carry them for the rest of their lives, the situation is brought home to you. I was ashamed and humiliated to think it was necessary for these young Canadian boys, many of them still only in their twenties, to come to Ottawa to appear before the veterans affairs committee and plead their case on behalf of themselves and their comrades, many of whom have still more serious disabilities. This thought ran through my mind: what member of that committee sitting around the tables would for one minute consider trading his whole body, with all his limbs and faculties intact, with that of one of these boys for the sum of $100 a month which they were asking to cover their serious disabilities? I may be entirely wrong in my opinion and judgment, but when I saw those boys and heard them plead their case I felt that $100 a month was a very small sum. Several of these 100 per cent disability cases spoke to the committee, and I should like to read briefly from what one of them said. It appears at page 337 of the proceedings of the committee for April 23. That veteran said:
May I say a word? After all, I am one of those chaps about whom you are talking. In 1M7, because I was an able-bodied citizen of this country, I was able to be in the front line at Vimy Ridge. At three o'clock one morning, on a raid, because I was able-bodied, had good eyesight, good arms, good legs, I lost two eyes and one arm. Now, I would not have anybody in this country think for one minute that there is enough money in the country to compensate me for what I lost. I want that very clearly understood. There is not enough money in the country. When I joined the services, I volunteered against the better judgment of my employer because I was a war worker. I volunteered because I thought it was the manly thing to do, and I still think I did the manly thing. So strongly do I hold those views that my children served in the last war. Now, that is one thing.
The salary I left was greater than this grateful country has given me as a pension in the
last thirty years. Now, I have taken it. I have never peddled my disability but I am going to say right here and now that the thing which kept me going was my loyalist background and the guts my ancestors gave me, not what the government did for me.
Others of these boys spoke before the committee, but I need not comment upon their remarks, because all the members heard them and could form their own opinions. That same day a very fine brief was presented by Mr. A. J. Wickens, K.C., dominion president of the army, navy and air force veterans. I was very much impressed with his presentation, and in his opening remarks he brought to the attention of the committee a matter which perhaps had not occurred to those members who did not belong to the legal profession. I should like to read a short paragraph from his remarks:
In approaching the question of the disabilities that follow from war casualties, I suppose a reasonable number of this committee are members of my profession, the profession of law, and will know the elements that are considered when you are assessing damages arising out of injuries received in civilian life. In civilian life there are six bases of estimating damages. The first is the loss of earning power from the disability, the permanent injury. That is under the heading of loss of income. The second is the loss of employability. The third is depreciation of the prospects of marriage. . . . The fourth is loss of participation in social activities and sports. The fifth is a most important one,
. . . the shortening of his expectation of life. The sixth one which enters into a civilian claim is pain and suffering which inevitably follow injuries.
With all those six items which enter in varying degrees into the damage which an individual suffers when he is injured, there is only one of them that has ever been considered as a basis for war disability allowance compensation. That is the first one, loss of income.
The fourth of the points so ably presented by Mr. Wickens was the loss of participation in social activities and sports. I remember one young veteran telling me that, when he appeared before the pension commission, because of his disabilities he knew he would never again take part in any sports. He mentioned what sports had meant to him in the past, and what this would mean to him in future. He was rather abruptly told that anything of that kind was not taken into consideration in any way. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that is an important point, because when a veteran suffers a disability as a result of which he may never again be able to participate in sports of which he was very fond, he will have to change his whole mode of living.
I need not comment further on the evidence given before the committee, except to say
Pension Act

that in my opinion the veterans who appeared with the various delegations presented a perfect case. It was well argued, and the exhibits were right there before our eyes. These exhibits were described by Padre Lambert as his "shattered fragments,'' and one only had to look at these shattered fragments to realize that the boys had proved their case to the very hilt, and that certainly $100 a month was not an extreme amount. However, the government has not seen fit to increase the basic rate of pension to that amount. All I can say is that the public of Canada, the parents, the wives, the dependents of the veterans and the veterans themselves will pass their own judgment on this decision by the government.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I was pleased to hear the minister announce this afternoon that the recommendations with respect to certain objectionable features in the Pension Act, such as wilful and deliberate concealment, the record on the medical sheet, the benefit of the doubt, the deadline re marriage, and the stabilization of world war I pensions were acceptable to the minister and the government. I suggest that, as soon as this bill is passed, the minister arrange to have the pension commission review all cases in which the decision was affected in any way by these various provisions which now are being struck out of the act.

speechtext:
Unfortunately when the minister made his statement this afternoon I was not in the house, but was attending the meeting of another committee. However, one of the hon. members has kindly given me a copy of the amendments that are to be moved when the sections of this bill are under discussion. Before proceeding to make my remarks, which will be brief, I should like to say that as a member of the committee I appreciated very much the regular attendance of the minister and the kind and courteous way in which he approached every question with which the committee dealt or which individual members had to bring up. I also want to say a word in appreciation of the work of the chairman of the committee. I think he is doing an excellent job. It is true that he has attempted to discipline me a few times, but in my opinion the chairman has been very fair, and has guided the committee in an excellent maner. It is a pleasure to serve on this committee. Regardless of party affiliations, I know the first concern of every member is the welfare of the veterans of this country. I must also pay tribute to the excellent presentations made by the two

large veterans' organizations, the Canadian Legion and the national council of veterans.
I am going to be brief, Mr. Chairman, because I want the bill to pass as quickly as possible, so that those people throughout the country who are looking forward to this extra 25 per cent will receive their cheques just as soon as they can be issued. While I fully appreciate the arguments which have been put forward by other hon. members in support of an increase greater than 25 per cent, I must say I am delighted that the government has seen fit to accept the unanimous recommendation of the committee for an increase of 25 per cent in pensions.
I might say on this point that I should like to make an explanation, in fairness to members of the C.C.F. group in the house. I have been informed that, while the debate was taking place this afternoon, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) made an interjection which indicated that a member of the C.C.F. group opposed the 33 j per cent increase, and another amendment for a greater increase than 25 per cent. That is not correct.
I am not at present officially a member of the C.C.F. group, and I voted for the 25 per cent increase in pensions. I did so because I was the mover of the motion for the 25 per cent increase in pensions. My motion was seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). That is why I supported the 25 per cent increase.

You know, Mr. Chairman, these hon. gentlemen who surround me are really frightened about the C.C.F., and they express it in minor ways.
I wish now to deal with the amendments which the minister suggested. They are:
1.	The deletion of the phrase "wilfully and deliberately concealed" from section 11(1) (c) of the Pension Act, and the inclusion of a definition for the phrase "recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment."
This is not exactly what the committee recommended, but. I for one am delighted indeed to see the deletion of the words "wilfully and deliberately concealed". I am sure members of the committee appreciate

The main feature of Bill No. 126 is the provision for an increase in the basic rate of pension, over which there has been so much1 controversy. I have in my hand the April, 1948, issue of the Labour Gazette, which is published monthly by the Department of Labour. Many things have happened in the past few weeks. We all remember the controversy we had in this chamber over the increase of 21 per cent in freight rates right across the board. For many of the people living in seven of the provinces of Canada the increase is actually more than 21 per cent. In the committee I cited the case of a young chap

who was operating a poultry farm under the Veterans Land Act. The rate to ship a 15-dozen crate of eggs was increased from thirty-five cents to seventy-five cents, or 114 per cent. I had the privilege at one time of serving on a municipal council. It is my opinion that the type of government closest to the problems of the people is the municipal government. They have to deal with the daily problems of the people. They are usually a hard-fisted lot of people who watch where the dollars are being spent. They are a taxing body, and it is interesting to note that many of these bodies across Canada have sent resolutions to this government asking for an increase of 33j per cent, which would raise the basic rate from $75 to $100. We should not overlook the fact that so many of these taxing bodies asked for the 33i per cent increase.
As was so well stated this afternoon, it is amazing the way in which the standard of living in this country has changed from 1925 up to the present time. There are many things that people require today which were hardly available in 1925. Many more things are necessary in the home and the cost of these things is not counted in making up the cost of living index.
I am sure we all appreciate the government going as far as they have in this, especially in view of the attitude of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Veterans Affairs earlier in the session and on other occasions. I have made reference this evening to the dates and incidents. This increase will be appreciated, but it is still far short of meeting the increased cost of living of many veterans and their dependents, and this cost is still rising every day. Much of the cost is the result of legislation passed by this House of Commons within the past few weeks.
I think I have said enough to substantiate our asking for the 33^ per cent increase. As was pointed out on other occasions, it is expected that when the budget is presented next week a surplus of approximately $800 million will be shown for the past fiscal year. Thousands of these people have done so much to save democracy for us. In view of what is happening in other countries throughout the world, I am sure that we appreciate our way of life today on the North American continent. Surely we might have granted this increase.
The increase agreed to will mean another $18,000,000 per year, but the increase asked for would have meant only an additional $6,000,000, or a total of $24,000,000. That does not seem a great amount when we hear the Department of Finance boasting daily about this great surplus which has been taken out of the people by taxation and which is expected to amount to approximately $800 million for the past fiscal year.
Like the previous speakers, I want to see this measure put through so that the cheques may be sent out just as rapidly as possible. I know these people will appreciate the increase they are getting, meagre as it is when compared with what we think they should rightfully have..

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because I think there has never been a time, during my parliamentary career in any event, when the civilian branch of our population has been so much interested in the increases of pensions and other disability compensation which normally should come to the veterans of both wars. That is evidenced by the fact that increases have been endorsed, as stated by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) a moment ago, not only by resolutions from municipal taxing bodies all over Canada but by every kind of conceivable organization composed of both men and women throughout the country who have been most emphatic in their pleas to the administration to give what they consider is nothing less than a square deal to the veterans of Canada.
I often think those of us who were not privileged to serve in either war should not allow the veterans of either war or both wars to cariy the whole load in their plea and claim for better compensation, for higher pensions and for greater allowances, because it is not just a veteran's problem. Primarily it is a veteran's problem, but it is also a problem which is part and parcel of the whole of the Dominion of Canada, and it is time that the civilian population of this dominion should team up with our veterans organizations and our veterans generally to see to it that we march together as a great Canadian nation seeking to do justice to the veterans and not allow the whole burden and obligation to fall upon those who have served. They have given much to this country in the past, and for that reason I think we who have not served have a definite obligation to see to it that we lend them our support, not just in mere talk, but in doing everything we possibly can to see that the veteran to whom we promised so much during each of the wars shall not feel

Pension Act
that those promises have in any respect not been carried out by the population who were not privileged to fight.
In my own case, as most know, several medical doctors in both wars prevented me from taking .any part in either one. For that reason I was not on the veterans affairs committee; but I did think this was a proper opportunity, in view of the fact that civilians all over the dominion are so much aroused on this question, that there should be a voice raised by someone who is not a veteran in support of the pleas which have so eloquently and so properly been made by our soldier members.
Some who are not familiar with parliamentary procedure may perhaps raise the question why, when the motion made in the yeterans affairs committee by my fellow member the hon. member for Royal, supported by others from this and other parties, for a 33! per cent increase in the pension rates was turned down in the veterans affairs committee, a similar motion is not made here to make the 33! per cent increase effective. I think the public ought to know that the rules of this committee prevent that. Otherwise the motion would be made, because that is the position which has been taken and it is one with which I am proud to associate myself as a civilian.
A minimum pension of 1100 a month for a 100 per cent disability pensioner has been endorsed by almost every civilian organization across our land, and a 33! per cent increase in the basic pension has been endorsed wholeheartedly and unanimously by the taxpaying people of Canada and our organized citizenry everywhere. During the wars there were no questions raised about how much we could spend to win those wars, and now the human instruments who won those wars have a just and proper claim that money and financial obstacles should no more be allowed to stand in the way of their getting justice than they were allowed to stand in the way of our winning the war when it was being fought, because after all, Mr. Chairman, this claim is just part and parcel of the payment we still must make for the winning of both wars. The two claims cannot be separated; they are inseparable, and for that reason, among others, I think we should so far as possible try to raise the pension rates up to the amounts which have been suggested.
The government has made some moves which have been acceptable so far as they go. I am going to make still one more plea to the minister, who I know has the interest of the veterans at heart, and that is to see to it, before we go any farther in connection with this matter, that we take public opinion as it 
is. You will have no trouble with public opinion; that is the last thing you need worry about. Governments often base their policies on public opinion. In this case there is nothing to fear. The public will not stop you or place any obstacles in your way. The public will endorse the government's action if it will now say that the pension shall be increased by 33! per cent and that there shall be a minimum of $100 a month for the 100 per cent disability pensioner. There is nothing standing in the way, and so I urge the government now to take that stand. I urge it on behalf of the great civilian population of Canada, who, with the veterans, I assure the government are definitely and wholeheartedly behind that step.
In connection with the stabilization of pensions for the first world war, one hears everywhere, not just among veterans, but among civilians who perhaps have not been as close to veterans affairs as others have been privileged to be, that the time has come, so far as veterans of the first world war particularly are concerned, to wipe out once and for all the red tape in connection with their pensions and war veterans allowances. What I mean by red tape is this. I think the time has come- and I am hopeful that the minister in his amendments will deal with this; indeed I have been told that it is to be one of his proposals, and if it is it will have our wholehearted support because it is a proper move and long overdue-when we should by legislation declare that never again shall there be an examination by any doctors of a pensioner of the first great rvar, aimed at reduction of pension. Call off the doctors, so far as trying to bring about a reduction in his pension is concerned. Surely, after all the veteran has gone through, it stands to reason that now, after all these years, there cannot be much improvement in the health of the veteran who served in the first world war.
One of the reasons I have been prompted to rise tonight and mention this is the case of a veteran in my own constituency. I shall not deal with it except to illustrate a general principle. This veteran for years upon years fought to get a pension following his service in the first world war. Less than a year ago he got that pension, and then within the last three or four weeks he found that his pension had been reduced as a result of another medical examination. After twenty years of fighting to get a pension, he was granted it, and then, within a few short months, the medical examiners reduced his pension by a considerable amount. Those things should not happen. It is that kind of thing which makes trouble

Pension Act
so far as our society is concerned. The dollars and cents involved matter nothing to the taxpayers of this country, who can well afford to give a square deal to the men who made it possible for us to pay the taxes and to be here and live in a democratic country.
And so I conclude with this. I know it is out of order, Mr. Chairman, but I shall be finished before you can call me to order. So far as the war veterans allowance is concerned, I think we might well wipe out the red tape there too, and when the minister brings down his amendments dealing with that, let us get rid of the infernal means test. Abolish it altogether so far as the recipients of the war veterans allowance are concerned. Case after case of hardship has been brought to my attention, and I say to the minister and to the government: The public is behind you if you will make a move in that direction. Public opinion will support you if you will give the veterans of this country their 33J per cent increase and the minimum of $100 a month for a 100 per cent disability. I know whereof I speak, because I have never seen the civilian population of Canada so aroused and so conscious, yes, and so ready to support to the last ditch the justified and legitimate claims of the men who fought for us and made it possible for us to carry on in this democracy.

This Bill No. 126, Mr. Chairman, received its first reading in the house on March 8. At that time some of us enumerated what we considered to be some of its shortcomings and suggested that the minister and those who were to serve on the committee might give study to some of the things we mentioned, with the end in view of bringing in amendments to cure those shortcomings. Not being a member of the committee, I find myself at a disadvantage in discussing the bill. A great many amendments have been made to Bill No. 126. Except to a few members who were on the committee, the amendments are not available. Actually most of us are discussing something we do not know anything about, or at least something we have not seen. Before the bill came back to the house to be discussed and put into final shape, I think it should have been reprinted so that the amendments would be contained in it. Had that been done, each and every member of the house would have some knowledge of exactly what the bill contains. The minister indicates that there is a desire to get it through as fast as possible, and so forth and so on. I am
never in a hurry to put anything through. I am always anxious to see that the job is done right, so that we shall not have any regrets afterwards.
With respect to the 25 per cent increase, I do not think we have done a great deal in that regard. I think the recommendation should have been: 100 per cent pension, $100. When it is considered that the great majority of pensioners are in the category of anywhere from 15 per cent to 35 per cent disability, the amount of money involved in the 25 per cent increase will not be so great. I think the yardstick by which we must measure that pension is whether or not it has any relationship to the cost of living. It must be remembered that in determining matters of this kind we are fixing standards and we are asking a man who is 100 per cent disabled to accept a standard of living of less than $100 a month.
I do not think any member of this house, either single or married, would say that would be a decent standard of living for himself and his family, if he had been totally incapacitated in the service of his country. These men are in that condition because they offered their lives in order to maintain institutions such as the one we are in here tonight; and I do not think we can clap ourselves on the back and say that 25 per cent increase is adequate, and establishes any kind of decent standard for those who are 100 per cent disabled.
Back in 1940 and many years before that, the minister and the veteran members of this house will remember the difficulty we had in determining pension cases where the doctor could say, "Well, this disability is of congenital origin; it was a constitutional defect" and for that reason, or for psychiatric reasons, the man was ruled out, and no pension given. We quarreled for years over that particular clause.
In 1940 the pension committee of this House of Commons removed that clause from the act. I was a member of that committee, and I had in mind at that time that we were removing from the act something which was a thorn in the side of those who administered the act, and had been for a great many years. I thought that, when this war was over, the veterans coming back would not be faced with that business of, "Well, despite the fact that you are in this condition, it is something that is hereditary; it is of congenital origin." That went out. Nevertheless that attitude is still being maintained. It is maintained in the decision now that the disability was of preenlistment origin. It is merely changing the wording. The administration is exactly the same.
I am thinking now in terms of the fact that 25 per cent of all medical discharges from the
Pension Act

army in this war were men who came out because of being broken down physically. They were not the calibre of people who were built to stand the stress and strain of war. They were discharged as psychopathic cases and no disability was recognized in that particular category. The man is placed in an institution. The fact of the matter is that the man is a war disability. His services were requisitioned by his country; he was placed in abnormal circumstances, and if he was not able to stand that kind of thing the responsibility was on the doctor who classified him as 100 per cent fit for service. I am disappointed that something definite and specific has not been written into the act at this time, stating that if a man was declared fit for service on a certain date and went into the service, and did not come out in the same physical condition, the wreckage caused during the interval should be attributable to war service for pension purposes. That is what is done in Britain. There is no quibbling about it there, and that is what should be done here. By leaving this question unsolved we are simply side-stepping the issue. You will have a number of them from the old country. Girls are going back now to get divorces in England, and the men are left here in Canada. What is their status? What is the status of the children who are left behind? They have no status. Our own divorce laws are rigid and restricted, and perhaps they should be; lam not arguing that point. I do say, however, on behalf of all those who served, that something should be done to protect the widows, the dependents and the soldiers themselves through the medium of this Pension Act; and it has not been done. There is no need to study the matter; it is not something new. I have gone over it all with the chairman of the pension commission, who was good enough to have the files brought in and to sit down and go over them with me. The facts are known. It is merely a matter of facing up to the problem and doing something about it. To have a committee study the matter and bring in a report of some kind next year is, in my opinion, just a way of side-stepping the matter in the hope that Divine Providence may solve the difficulty in the meantime. Well, things just don't happen like that.
Another matter I think we overlooked is the question of merchant marine service for pension purposes. They are covered now

under the civilian personnel provisions of the Pension Act, but that coverage is very much restricted. You almost have to prove that a man suffered a direct hit from a torpedo before you can get a pension for him. There are men going around with legs off, casualties of war, for whom pension cannot be established. I think we should have gone at least as far as to grant them pensions. We have denied them every other privilege that has been granted other members of the armed services. We have refused to give them any status whatever along those lines, with one or two minor exceptions. We did, however, make a feeble gesture toward them in the matter of disability pensions, and I think we should have gone all the way with it. We should have given them exactly the same protection and the same latitude in the matter of disability compensation that we gave those in the armed services, but we have not done so. They remain as they were. In my opinion they performed some of the greatest service ever seen, but unfortunately they served private shipping companies who merely exploited them during the war, made what profits they could and assumed no responsibility for the wreckage of war. I think at least we should have included them in this act for disability pension purposes.
Another defect that has not been corrected is, I believe, in connection with the disability pension dying with the pensioner. As the situation now is, if a man receiving a pension of fifty per cent or better passes away, that pension is continued to his wife and dependents. If the pension is under fifty per cent, however, it dies with the pensioner. I think, to be fair about it, if a man is receiving even a five per cent or a ten per cent pension it should be continued to his dependents after his death, because in my opinion the recipient of a small pension often leaves his family in worse circumstances than one in receipt of a pension of fifty per cent or more. I think it would have been only fair and just and reasonable if the committee had recommended an amendment continuing payment of these disability pensions, no matter what might be the percentage of the pension. That provision would be there, then, as a matter of right; but that has not been done.

Mr. Chairman, I did not have an opportunity to be a member of the veterans affairs committee. I have not had a chance to study the bill as closely as some may have had, nor have I had a chance to speak on it until now.
Some hon. members have mentioned the number of petitions they have received from their constituencies. Let me say that I never have received so many resolutions on any subject-and I include price controls and railways-from boards of trade, municipal councils and veterans' organizations as I have had in support of the plea for $100 a month for 100 per cent disability cases.
After every session, when I return home I hold meetings at different points in my constituency, and in those meetings I attempt to explain the legislation of the session. In this instance I do not know what I am going to tell my constituents, because there does not seem to me to be any reason for not giving $100 a month. In my view the only question we should ask is this: Can health and decency be maintained on any less than $100 a month? The answer of course is no. With the cost of living at present levels, no one can live in decency or comfort on less than $100 a month. So that, in itself, condemns anything less than $100 a month as a pension.
Pension Act

The second question is: Can Canada afford $100 a month? The answer is, yes. If $100 is not enough, and we have the money, why are we paying less? Surely there is no justification for what we are doing. Certainly there is none, so far as I can see.
Some mention has been made of impassioned speeches on behalf of the veterans. I say any plea made on behalf of the veterans could not begin to compare with the enlistment pleas, the bands, the speeches and the publicity which went out warning us that our country was in danger-and it was-and that it would fall, as it would have, if these men had not given life and limb and health in the defence of our country.
Now when our country is intact, when our industries are more productive than ever, when our agriculture is geared to a new high in production, when we have markets and income and production, what possible justification can there be for denying a decent living to those men who made all this possible? I can see no justice or logic in the government's position.
It is time we got away from the old idea of charity in connection with these pensions. We still think in. terms of a hand-out. This is not a case of charity; it is a case of simple justice. Anything less than comfort and decency is a reflection not only upon the veterans but upon our own consciences, and upon our record as a nation. So I plead with the minister, even at this late day, to reconsider the sum mentioned, and to give at least a minimum of $100 a month for 100 per cent disability.
Again I voice the sentiments of the hon. member who said a few moments ago that public opinion would be behind the minister if he were to do that. The cost of living index stands at an all-time high for Canada. It is more than 151 at the present time, and is still going up. We are told that the price of meat is to increase, and there is no indication whatsoever that we shall have a return to price controls. Increased freight rates will certainly increase the cost of everything that has to be shipped-and that is everything; period. That includes meat, wheat, bread-everything; and there is no indication that these prices will come down.
The housing bill brought from the minister the other night a statement to the effect of rentals at $80 a month, This sort of living allowance must mean, therefore, that a veteran will have to live in the worst street, in the worst house, on the poorest of food and with the poorest of cultural and recreational 
facilities at his disposal. Surely that is shabby treatment for the people who made the present prosperity in Canada a reality.
There is no reason why the families of these men should have the poorest clothes or live under the poorest living conditions on the street. And that is what you are condemning these families to, when you condemn them to that sort of living.
A further point to be considered is that these pension moneys would go immediately into the spending stream in Canada. They will help maintain employment. This is not the kind of income which would be saved and salted away. It is a type of income which, along with family allowances and old age pensions, will be poured into the stream of everyday spending to maintain our Canadian economy at a high level.
So I plead with the minister even at this day to do something about granting this request, so just, so fair and so reasonable.

Mr. Chairman, just before the bill carries, I should like to say a word or two. In a general way there is some cause for the country to take comfort when it looks over what we are doing for our men of world war II as compared with what we did for the men who came home from world war I. But our efforts are still far short of what they should be.
The vote on the 33i per cent increase in the veterans affairs committee was, I am told,

as follows: fifteen voted for and sixteen voted against the 33i per cent increase. The veterans throughout the country and their parents and loved ones across Canada can derive comfort from that fact, because it shows how the realization of Canada's responsibilities is gradually dawning upon the members of this house. I am glad to say, and I am saying this for the sake of Social Crediters all across the dominion, that the Social Credit members of the committee all voted for that 33i per cent increase. I think every member of the Social Credit party throughout the dominion, if he had been a member of that committee, would have voted for that 33J per cent increase. If this house consisted of Social Credit members they would have voted for that 33^ per cent increase and a good deal more than that.
Too many members of this house, Mr. Chairman, I fear, still fail to appreciate the realities of the situation as regards the veterans and Canada's responsibilities to them. Let us rc-member that before these boys put on the king's uniform every one of them was a potential husband and father. He probably was a preferred man with the girls of his community. When a good many of those boys came back they had very little chance of finding favour in the eyes of those girls, much as the girls might have sympathized with them, because they were broken. Every one of those boys once had a potential career before him. Now, as a result of what they went through, for many of them there can be no career. We cannot give them a career, but we can, if we treat them fairly in respect of financial considerations, give them something like a chance to become husbands and fathers.
May I say once more what I have said several times on the floor of this house. This Dominion of Canada at the present time cannot afford to disregard potential husbands and fathers. This country needs babies, and it needs many of them. I am amazed that one or two people are smiling in the face of what I am saying. Cannot hon. members be realistic? It has often been pointed out that a small population like ours of 12,000,000 people cannot hope to hold such a magnificent heritage as Canada is without having the necessary population. There is only one way to get good Canadian population, and that is to raise them. Why not face that fact and look upon all these boys as potential husbands and fathers? We can make of them, so long as they have lived decently, husbands and fathers if we will only use the financial means with which to do so. Surely we ought to do that even in our own best

Pension Act
interests as a Canadian people, without considering the veteran himself at all. This is one thing to which we should give serious consideration.
Let us briefly examine the increase which has been given. I do not wish to minimize that increase at all, but let us face the facts and give it something like a correct appraisal. The pension, as it was before the present increase, was approved in 1925, and was at that time considered by the good people who then sat in this house a fairly adequate allowance for the veteran. But. what has happened since 1925? The ordinary labourer in those days received 100; I am using that as an index figure. The ordinary labourer in 1947 received 197-4. In other words the ordinary labourer on the street has been able to increase his earnings by 97-4 per cent since 1925. But these veterans, choice men who went overseas, and who were the best we had and were taken over there because they were the best, are deemed to be not worth any more than a 25 per cent increase. How can ordinary members put those figures together and get sense?
Again, living costs have risen from 100 in 1925 to 125-9. Apparently that 25-9 has been the figure which has been in the minds of those who, with meticulous care, limited the size of this pension increase.
But they have utterly disregarded a good many other factors. The purchasing power of the pension, which was 100 in 1925, had already fallen to 79-4 before this increase That is, before we increased the pension, we were giving veterans only 79-4 per cent of what the same pension was in 1925. So that the 25 per cent increase is actually 25 per cent of 79-4 per cent of the 1925 pension. That is a serious matter to bear in mind. Meanwhile the purchasing power of unskilled labour had risen from 100 in 1925 to 142-2 in March, 1948.
I notice that in all those figures which were provided for members of the veterans affairs committee, of which I was not fortunate enough to be a member, a great many of the little things which are essentials, which are almost "musts," are disregarded. For example, the ordinary man wants to go to a barber and get a haircut. So the ordinary veteran of course wishes to indulge himself in the luxury of having a good haircut by a skilled barber. But what has happened to the price of haircuts since 1925? In 1925 you could get a good haircut for thirty-five cents. What do you pay today for a good haircut? Fifty or sixty cents.
I am not sure that a man had to provide his wife with a hair-do in 1925, but today in any home the wife becomes unhappy if she is unable to have a hair-do once in a while to make her look something like the other girls with whom she associates.
The veteran has no consideration in little matters of that sort which figure so largely in the emotional life of the people, the girls they marry, and their daughters as they grow up.
Here is another little thing, but a thing we should not overlook. In 1925 the very best show would cost about twenty-five cents. Today you pay between fifty and sixty cents for the same kind of show with a tax included, and I do not suppose there would be any provision for relieving the veteran of the necessity of paying that tax on theatre tickets. It is callous to say that veterans do not need to go to shows. Are these men who went through the hell of war, whose minds are filled with horrible pictures, too terrible even for them to turn and glance at occasionally-they almost faint when they look at some of the pictures of things that they were obliged to look at in those terrible days-to be forbidden the privilege of going to shows just because they went and fought and saw horrible scenes which have been stamped indelibly on their minds? These are things which affect the lives of our men.
Let us remember that in the recent war we had a nation at arms; practically the full manhood of this nation was under arms. Therefore, when we are dealing with veterans we are dealing almost with Canada. Everything we put in this bill is affecting the veteran and the veteran's wife and children and his dependents, all over this nation from coast to coast. It is no small matter. Although I commend the minister and the veterans affairs committee on the fine work they have done, yet I feel that they should go right to work the day after this bill is passed and revise the act and have it all ready for us when we get back here next session. The new revision should be on adequate lines.
One thing comes to my mind. This bill, notwithstanding that the disabilities and the disadvantages which I have already indicated in it were sufficiently glaring, fails utterly to recompense the men for the suffering which they have gone through. Many of these men go through excruciating suffering.
One man came into my office just the other day. He is one of the men on the staff of messengers. He had a beautiful band of ribbons on his breast. We asked him how he
Pension Act

was feeling. He said that he had quite a lot of rheumatism in one of his feet. We asked him one or two little questions and he said, "Well, not all the men have had to sleep, where I have had to sleep". We elicited from that man that he had been through the Sicily campaign and the Italian campaign. He is an illustration. Yet he is relatively fortunate. No matter what financial considerations we give, we do not make any reimbursement for that suffering. We do not make restitution for the disfiguration, the humiliation and the conspicuousness that the men feel when they are disfigured, when they know that every step they take or every move they make they are noticed by everybody. Too many members of this committee do not know what it is to have a physical disability; and unfortunately for the disfigured veterans, a good many of the returned men who were elected to this house, who were sent here to help the returned men out, did not receive any disablement at all. If the people had sent the disabled to this house to tell us how disabled men feel after a war, probably more consideration would have been given than is being given by some of the boys who went through the war with scarcely a serious injury.
There is no recompense for the unhappiness. I referred to that a minute or two ago. Consider those who have been right in close, the veterans who went right through the hell of the thing, went right through those awful scenes, saw men, for instance, blown to pieces by booby traps, or who hastily scratched the soil over fallen comrades in order that the morale of the men following would not be destroyed. They did that hour after hour! They think of the awful scenes. You can do nothing to eradicate from the minds of such men the horrible pictures. You cannot remedy the distortion of their personalities, wrought by such things in their minds all the time. Many of these'men will almost jump out of bed at night or scream aloud, because their minds in dreams are working around some of the awful things they went through. We are doing nothing to recompense these men for these dreadful things. If we gave everything they asked in the way of money we would still be deeply in debt to the ordinary soldier for what he went through over there.
Under the circumstances, I feel that we ought to have let the boys have what they
asked for. After all, they were moderate enough in their request. They said, "Give us S100 for full disability; give us 33^ per cent"! Well, all we would have had to do would be to give them $72 more a year, and we would be giving them what they asked for. Instead of that, we told them what we thought they ought to have; and we are giving them what we think they ought to have, instead of what they ask for.
